author: Carlos Martinez
title: Racing Clean Against Dirty Drivers: Strategy and Survival
description: Learn how to race competitively without matching aggressive tactics. Protect your safety rating while staying fast on track.

sections.p: Racing clean when the other driver is not puts you in a bind. You want to race hard, defend your position, hold your line. But matching their aggression costs you incidents, safety rating, and iRating. The solution is not to back out of the fight. It is to race smart: predictable lines, defensive positioning, and a clear decision about when to yield and when to hold.

Dirty racing in iRacing comes in a few forms. Some drivers bump others on the exit of slow corners to gain a tow. Some dive to the inside with no real speed and hope for contact. Some weave across the track to break your rhythm on the straights. Others simply refuse to yield and turn in on you when they are alongside. Each requires a different response, and the goal is to stay clean yourself while making it as hard as possible for them to gain from their tactics.

The fastest way to lose a battle with a dirty driver is to panic and change your line erratically. They are betting on confusion and the chaos of contact. A predictable line is the opposite. When a driver knows exactly where you will be on corner entry, mid-corner, and exit, they cannot rely on a bump to work. A clean driver who commits to a single, smooth line and hits every mark becomes harder to pass by brute force.

This means staying in your normal line even when you see an aggressive car approaching. Do not suddenly move left or right to block a passing attempt before it begins. Do not brake earlier than usual or trail off the throttle to give them more room. Both make you unpredictable and invite a collision. Instead, brake at your normal point, turn in at your normal angle, and exit at your normal speed. If they cannot make the pass without hitting you, they will either back out or make a mistake.

sections.tip: A driver who can anticipate your line five corners in advance will make better defensive decisions than one who reacts to their moves lap after lap.

sections.p: Defense is not the same as blocking, and iRacing stewards know the difference. Blocking means moving your car to a new position specifically to close off a passing lane. Defense means staying in the fastest line and using your position to deny speed on the approach to a corner. A clean defense protects the racing line, not the track width.

On a straight before a corner, if a car is alongside you, you have the right to your normal racing line on entry. If they are still there as you approach the braking zone, brake to your usual point. Do not move across to their side of the track to push them out. Let them go in deep, where they will either miss the apex or run off track. On the exit, you own the track again because you are on the correct line. A late braking defense that stays in your normal zone is legal and effective.

For chicanes and technical sections, the same principle applies. Take your normal line through the first turn and the second turn. If a driver behind you tries to thread a different path or cut a corner to gain an advantage, you do not need to block them. They will either go off track or hit you on an illegal line. Your job is to execute your line perfectly and let them make the mistake.

sections.h2: Reading the moment: When to hold and when to yield

sections.p: Not every pass is worth defending to the limit. A wise racer knows when to hold a position and when to yield to avoid an incident. The decision depends on your safety rating buffer, the gap to the next car, and the likelihood of a clean outcome.

list: Hold a position if the gap ahead is more than a second or two. A dirty pass here costs you places but not the race. If they hit you and you both spin, you lose more time than a single position.
Yield into a slow corner if they have a run on you from two car lengths back. A T1 pile-up is not worth staying in a provisional lead.
Defend into a high-speed section if you are ahead and your line is committed. Speed favors the driver ahead. A dirty driver cannot make a high-risk pass here without real jeopardy.
Yield on a short straight before a technical section. If they are close enough to hit you at 150 mph, an incident is likely even if you defend well.

sections.p: The goal is to lose as little as possible while maintaining your safety rating. A clean fourth place is better than a dirty second-place finish and a 3-incident penalty.

When multiple cars are fighting, a dirty driver has to be aware of the traffic around them. They are more likely to take risks if they think they can get away with it. Position yourself so that a dirty move has witnesses. Race where the stewards can see it, even though you are not literally watched in real time. In a large field, being visible to multiple cars means that aggressive driving is more likely to be protested later.

If a car behind the dirty driver is also close, they are less likely to dive bomb you going into a corner. They have to worry about someone hitting them from behind if they miss their mark. Use this to your advantage by not defending too hard when a third car is in the mix. Let the dirty driver do the risky thing and leave room for a following car to exploit their mistake.

sections.h2: Mental game: Not letting them get in your head

sections.p: The hardest part of racing clean against aggression is not letting frustration take over. A dirty driver wants you to panic, to make a mistake out of anger, or to retaliate and risk your rating yourself. Do not take the bait. Your iRating and safety rating are long term. This single race is not.

Focus on your own pace. Run your own line. If you finish behind them because they brake check you or bump you out of a corner, that is their incident to explain, not yours. If you hit them because you tried to retaliate, that incident is yours alone. The math is simple.

sections.tip: A protest filed after a race with clear contact and witness telemetry carries more weight than any in-the-moment reaction.

sections.h2: When to protest and when to move on

sections.p: If a driver hit you in a way that was clearly avoidable and cost you the race, a protest is fair. Video it. Note the lap and the turn. But protest only contact that was deliberate or grossly negligent. A misjudged dive brake where they hit you but also went off track is worth mentioning. A brake check that sends you into the wall is worth protesting. A slightly tight inside line that caused contact while you were both committed is a racing incident.

Stewards handle the evidence and the patterns. If a driver has a history of dirty moves, a single protest from you is part of a larger file. If a driver is clean in 99 other races and gets one incident with you, they will know it was an accident. Protest with evidence when it matters. Ignore the aggressive cars who are just bad at racecraft and will lose their iRating on their own.

faqs.q: Should I always yield to a dirty driver to protect my safety rating?
faqs.a: No. Yielding constantly teaches dirty drivers that aggression works and costs you positions you could have held cleanly. Defend your line and position predictably. Yield only when the risk of contact is high and the position is not critical to the race. A clean defense that they fail to execute is their incident, not yours.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a legal defense and blocking?
faqs.a: A legal defense uses your normal racing line to deny the passing lane. You brake where you normally brake, turn in where you normally turn in, and exit where you normally exit. Blocking means moving your car to a new position specifically to close off a pass that was already in progress. If your line would have taken you to that spot anyway, it is defense. If you moved to get there, it is blocking.

faqs.q: Can I retaliate against a driver who hit me, or will I get penalized?
faqs.a: Retaliation will cost you the same incidents and safety rating as the original contact, or worse. Even if their move was illegal, an intentional hit from you is also illegal. Race clean in the moment. File a protest after the race if the contact was deliberate or grossly negligent. That is the path to protecting your rating and punishing bad behavior.

faqs.q: How do I know if a close pass was dirty or just aggressive racing?
faqs.a: Dirty racing involves contact or a brake check designed to unsettle you. Aggressive racing is a hard, late-braking dive to the inside or a close run on the outside where both cars remain committed to the corner. A driver who passes you clean by being bolder or faster is not being dirty. A driver who bumps you or causes unavoidable contact to gain position is. Judge by the outcome and the commitment, not by how close they got.
